OKHWB v2 · staggered hues

48 source hues × 21 colored samples + 16 shared grays = 1,024 unique colors. The white/black lattice stays put; the hue changes from cell to cell. Your green-cell path keeps the source hue, while the yellow-dot counts spread the other samples toward the next 7.5° slice.

Your sketch, on the lattice

One green dot means no hue shift. Each yellow dot adds one hue step for that column. The dots describe one color per cell.

Read each column from white toward black. Its cells share W + B, and its step size is 7.5° divided by its number of cells. That gives larger angular steps toward the vivid tip, with the tip itself anchored.

The six columns have 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, and 1 cells. This follows the final drawing. Together they contribute 21 samples per source hue.

The shared grayscale

The same sixteen grays as v1: evenly spaced in OKHSV value, including black and white. Shown along each triangle edge, stored once.

Exact hue steps and measured distances

Keep W = i/6 and B = j/6 for nonnegative integers i + j < 6. In a column of n = i + j + 1 cells, take the dot count k from the table and set H = (source H + k × 7.5° / n) modulo 360. Steps run forward to, but exclude, the next source hue.

The conversion uses Ottosson’s OKHWB definition: OKHSV V = 1 − B and S = 1 − W/(1 − B), with black handled explicitly. Reference sRGB conversion, then nearest-byte rounding.

Hue staggering adds angular variety while preserving the original white/black steps. It does not promise smoother tonal steps or fewer perceptually close pairs. This version keeps the drawing’s geometry, without fitting, pruning, or fillers.

Cells are nearest-sample regions in the drawn W/B triangle. Their areas are not perceptual distances or gamut volumes.
